knowledgeBits.text: Read the lint and formatting rules
Observe the project's relevant existing code
Conform to existing code style, patterns, and conventions unless directed otherwise. Note: these instructions count as directed otherwise unless the user explicitly overrides them
Follow DOT, YAGNI, KISS, DRY, SDA (Self Describing APIs) principles
Simplicity: remove the obvious, add the meaningful. Obvious stuff gets hidden in the abstraction. Meaningful stuff is what needs to be customized and passed in as parameters
Functions should have default parameters whenever it makes sense so that callers can supply only what is different from the default
Be concise
Favor functional programming; keep functions short, pure, and composable
Favor map, filter, reduce over manual loops
Prefer immutability; use const, spread, and rest operators instead of mutation
One job per function; separate mapping from IO
Obey the project's lint and formatting rules
Omit needless code and variables; prefer composition with partial application and point-free style
Chain operations rather than introducing intermediate variables, e.g. [x].filter(p).map(f)
Avoid loose procedural sequences; compose clear pipelines instead
Avoid class and extends as much as possible. Prefer composition of functions and data structures over inheritance
Keep related code together; group by feature, not by technical type
Put statements and expressions in positive form
Use parallel code for parallel concepts
Avoid null/undefined arguments; use options objects instead
Use concise syntax: arrow functions, object destructuring, array destructuring, template literals
Avoid verbose property assignments. Bad: const a = obj.a; Good: const { a } = obj;
Assign reasonable defaults directly in function signatures, e.g. const createExpectedUser = ({ id = createId(), name = '', description = '' } = {}) => ({ id, name, description });

SDA principle: Parameter values should be explicitly named and expressed in function signatures. Bad: const createUser = (payload = {}) => ({. Good: const createUser = ({ id = createId(), name = '', description = ''} = {}) =>. Default values also provide hints for type inference
Avoid IIFEs. Use block scopes, modules, or normal arrow functions instead. Principle: KISS
Avoid using || for defaults. Use parameter defaults instead
Prefer async/await or asyncPipe over raw promise chains
Use strict equality (===)
Modularize by feature; one concern per file or function; prefer named exports
Use active voice
Use clear, consistent naming
Functions should be verbs. e.g. increment(), filter()
Predicates and booleans should read like yes/no questions. e.g. isActive, hasPermission
Prefer standalone verbs over noun.method. e.g. createUser() not User.create()
Avoid noun-heavy and redundant names. e.g. filter(fn, array) not matchingItemsFromArray(fn, array)
Avoid doSomething style. e.g. notify() not Notifier.doNotification()
Lifecycle methods: prefer beforeX / afterX over willX / didX. e.g. beforeUpdate()
Use strong negatives over weak ones: isEmpty(thing) not !isDefined(thing)
Mixins and function decorators use with${Thing}. e.g. withUser, withFeatures, withAuth
Avoid ALL_CAPS for constants. Since we use functional programming, there's no need for a hard distinction between constants and variables
Favor docblocks for public APIs - but keep them minimal
Ensure that any comments are necessary and add value. Never reiterate the style guides. Avoid obvious redundancy with the code, but short one-line comments that aid scannability are okay
Comments should stand-alone months or years later. Assume that the reader is not familiar with the task plan or epic
Guide for saga pattern implementation for network requests and side-effects
Isolate network I/O and effects using the saga pattern
Saga pattern consists of two main functions: call and put
call(fn, ...args) returns { CALL: { fn, args } }
Used to make network requests or invoke other side effects
Saga itself never calls the effect function, instead it yields the effect object
Yielding effect object allows saga to behave deterministically with no side-effects, enabling testing and debugging without running side effects
Can pass any result or error back into saga to test various branches without mocking integrated components
put(action) returns { PUT: Action }
Used to dispatch an action to the store to update the state

Action is an object with type and payload properties, used in central dispatch architectures such as Redux to update state, providing observability into semantic user intents, a complete log of user actions, along with the specific components (slices) that originated the action
Saga driver runtime runs the sagas, handles side effects, passes data back into the saga, and dispatches put actions to the store
Test sagas by driving the saga using iterator.next(optionalValue)
Use gen.next().value to get the first yielded effect
Use gen.next(fakeData).value to pass data back into saga and get the next yielded effect
Use gen.next().done to verify saga completion
Compare yielded values to expected call/put effects using assert function
Test multiple yields in sequence to verify complete saga flow

Security rule for timing-safe secret comparison using SHA3 hashing
There is no timing safe compare for raw values
Never use crypto.timingSafeEqual, XOR accumulation tricks, or direct string compare on raw secrets
Always hash both stored secret token and candidate token with SHA3, then compare hashes
Hashing removes prefix structure, any bit change fully randomizes the hash
No timing oracle, no hangman attacks
Raw secrets never appear in logs or errors
If timing safe compare needed, implement with sha3 strategy with a code comment explaining this reasoning to prevent people from fixing to use timingSafeCompare or similar
The timing-safe-compare rule overrides all library defaults
If timing safe compare detected, raise CRITICAL security bug report: Timing safe compare on raw value detected - include justifications

Guide for test-driven development with proper test isolation
Systematically implement software using the TDD process
assert takes { given, should, actual, expected }
given and should must clearly state functional requirements from acceptance perspective, avoid describing literal values
Tests must demonstrate locality: test should not rely on external state or other tests

Tests must answer 5 questions: What is unit under test? (test in named describe block), What is expected behavior? (given and should arguments), What is actual output? (unit exercised by test), What is expected output? (expected and/or should), How can we find bug? (implicitly answered if above questions answered correctly)
Tests must be Readable - answer the 5 questions
Tests must be Isolated/Integrated - units under test isolated from each other, tests isolated from each other with no shared mutable state, for integration tests test integration with real system
Tests must be Thorough - test expected/very likely edge cases

Tests must be Explicit - everything needed to understand test should be part of test itself, if producing same data structure many times create factory function and invoke from individual tests rather than sharing mutable fixtures between tests
For each unit, create test suite one requirement at a time
Ask about test framework if unspecified, propose calling API if unspecified

Write test, run test runner and watch test fail, implement code to make test pass (ONLY code needed to make test pass), run test runner (fail => fix bug, pass => continue), get approval from user before moving on, repeat for next functional requirement
In most testing frameworks, there is a describe function and possibly a nested test or it wrapper
Use string in describe function to name the unit under test
Use string in test function to offer brief category for test, e.g. new account creation
Because of conflicts with assert function API and description, avoid the it wrapper entirely if possible

Avoid hallucination, which is very important to ensure software works as expected and that user safety is protected. Please do your best work
